# Decoding Fault Code 27 on a '94 Jeep Cherokee XJ

Fault code 27 on a 1994 Jeep Cherokee with the 4.0L V6 engine is a specific diagnostic indicator: the Engine Control Module (ECM) has detected that the fuel injector circuit is not syncing with the input signal. In modern OBD-II parlance, this often translates to a "Fuel Trim" or "Injector Circuit Malfunction," but on the legacy 5.0L ECM found in these vehicles, the logic is slightly different. The computer expects a specific voltage pulse from the injector driver during its internal firing sequence. When it doesn't see the expected feedback within the allotted time window, it flags code 27.

This isn't just a "check engine light" issue; it means the fuel delivery timing or quantity is compromised. If you ignore this, the ECM will default to a fallback mode, likely enriching the fuel mixture significantly to ensure the engine doesn't stall. You might notice rough idling, hesitation during acceleration, or a distinct "chugging" sound from the intake manifold. The root cause usually lies in the electrical path between the ECM and the injector bank that failed to sync.

## Isolating the Faulty Injector Bank

The first step in troubleshooting is determining which bank of injectors is at fault. The 4.0L engine has two banks of fuel injectors (Bank 1 on the passenger side, Bank 2 on the driver's side), and the ECM monitors them somewhat independently regarding sync timing.

To isolate the issue without immediately replacing parts, you need to verify the physical connections and the state of the injector solenoids. Start by visually inspecting the wiring harness. The Jeep XJ is notorious for rodent damage or corroded connectors in the engine bay. Look specifically at the plugs near the firewall and the intake manifold. If you find a connector with corrosion or loose pins, that is your culprit. Cleaning and reseating these often resolves the sync error instantly.

If the wiring appears intact, you must test the injectors themselves. A common failure mode is an open circuit or high resistance within the injector coil, preventing it from activating when the ECM sends the pulse. You can perform a resistance check using a multimeter. Disconnect the electrical connector from one injector and measure the resistance across the two terminals at the bottom of the injector body.

Typical specifications for these GM-based injectors (often sourced from Chevrolet or GMC vehicles) range between 10 to 16 ohms, though exact values vary by manufacturer. If your multimeter reads infinite resistance (OL), the injector coil is open and must be replaced. If the reading is significantly lower than 10 ohms, the coil is shorted. A common pitfall here is testing the injectors while they are still connected to the harness; always disconnect the electrical plug before measuring resistance to avoid false readings caused by parallel circuit paths.

## Verifying the ECM and Power Supply

If all four injectors on a specific bank show normal resistance, but code 27 persists, the fault may lie with the ECM's internal driver circuit or the power supply feeding that bank. The ECM uses a "dual-rail" system for fuel injection in some configurations, where it switches between two voltage rails to fire the injectors. If the switching transistor inside the ECM fails open, that entire bank will fail to sync.

Before condemning the expensive ECM, verify the power and ground paths. Check the fuse protecting the fuel pump and the specific fuses dedicated to the injector control circuits in the engine compartment fuse box. A weak or intermittent ground connection at the chassis or engine block can also cause the ECM to misinterpret the signal as a missing sync. Trace the ground straps from the engine to the frame; ensure they are bolted tight and free of paint or rust that could insulate them.

## The Decision Matrix

When you have confirmed good wiring, good grounds, and functional injectors, you face a choice: replace the injector driver module (if it's an external component, though rare on these engines) or rebuild/replace the ECM. In many cases of code 27 on the '94 Cherokee, the ECM itself has suffered internal component failure.

However, before spending money on a new unit, consider that some aftermarket fuel systems or modified ignition setups might alter the firing timing enough to confuse the stock ECM's sync logic. If you have not recently modified your fuel system, stick to OEM parts. The trade-off here is cost versus risk; replacing the ECM is expensive, but running on a failing fuel system risks catastrophic engine damage if the engine runs lean or stalls unexpectedly under load.

Always clear the code after repairs and perform a drive cycle. On the 4.0L, the ECM requires a specific set of driving conditions to relearn fuel trims and verify that the injector circuits are now syncing correctly. If the light returns immediately after clearing, you likely have an intermittent electrical issue or a failing ground strap that wasn't fully addressed during the initial inspection.
